subsubtopic: STRENGTHENING OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Two days ago, at the U.S. Senate hearings on the confirmation of secretary of state-elect, Alexander Haig, the chairman of the foreign relations committee, senator Charles Percy, questioned Mr. Haig on the prospect of relations with Canada, especially in view of the east coast fisheries treaty. Both gentlemen obviously displayed positive approaches to strengthening these relations. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That this House applauds the constructive initiative taken by the chairman and welcomes this indication of more constructive co-operation between Canada and the United States in the years ahead, and expresses its profound chagrin that the Prime Minister of Canada chose to trade scallops for skiing when he refused to meet with president-elect Reagan.

speechtext:

cancelled altogether, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House urge the Government of Canada to accept the offer made to the Prime Minister by Premier Lougheed on July 25 last, and cancel the discriminatory taxes levied on the oil industry in the recent budget.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF PROJECTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the federal government, despite its verbal commitment to recognizing 1981 as the International Year of Disabled Persons, has allocated only $1 million to projects for the disabled in the current year, and has unfairly set January 15, or this Friday, as the closing date for applications for these funds, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the federal government extend the deadline for applications to at least February 15, 1981, since many groups cannot meet the Friday deadline, and that the government immediately increase the amount of funding beyond $1 million which is an inadequate sum to reflect the genuine feeling among many Canadians that 1981 must be the beginning of a new era for our handicapped population.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED RESOLUTION-AMENDMENT RESPECTING REFERENDA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of pressing necessity to every Canadian. Two days ago the government proposed certain amendments, one of which will clearly add to our national unity problems. I refer specifically to its proposed change to section 41, that there be in practice three classes of Canadians for purposes of constitutional amendments by referenda: first, Ontarians and Quebeckers; second, maritimers; third, westerners. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That every Canadian must have equal status in any consensus-gaining mechanism relating to constitutional amendments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all summer we had many negotiations with the provinces. We told them on June 9 that we were proceeding with patriation of the constitution and the enshrining therein of a bill of rights. We tried to reach an agreement all summer. This part of the constitutional package will be dealt with in the House of Commons.
When I replied to the question it was a question in relation to whether we should convene a new conference of first ministers. We said a long time ago that we do not think that would be useful. Of course, when the constitution is patriated and we have a bill of rights in the constitution, we have said there will be a resumption of the meetings with the provinces to look at all the other aspects of the constitutional problems that face the nation. There was a list on the table last summer of other items which must be discussed, like the position of native people in the constitution, and so on. We will be willing to resume our negotiations with the provinces after the work of this House on the first phase is completed.

subsubtopic: EFFECTS OF MONETARY POLICIES-ADJUSTMENT OF RATE OF INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I direct my supplementary question to the Minister of Finance. As the government bulldozes its way unilaterally to Westminster, the great fear that we have is that the Minister of Finance and the government are forgetting the consequences of their monetary policies and their policies in general on the working poor of this country, the one million unemployed and the old age pensioner. Food prices are rising and will be, for example, further exacerbated by the inclement weather conditions in the southern United States. The price of eggs has gone up and the high interest rates will work their way into the food system. If the minister has his priorities correct, what steps does the government intend to take now in order to alleviate the suffering of these millions of Canadians?

subsubtopic: MR. FRIESEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. DUCLOS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I regret that I have to draw to your attention a matter which occurred some time ago. I gave notice of it to you, Madam Speaker, before Christmas. It has to do with the conduct of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Duclos) who has been absent most of the time, so this is the first opportunity I have on which to bring it to your attention.
My question of privilege has to do with the question I raised in the House prior to the Christmas recess regarding the deafening silence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the matter of the fears of the western world of the Soviet Union in relation to Poland.
My question was raised in the adjournment debate and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs answered it at the time. It seems to me that his response was deliberately designed to stifle debate in that he tried to intimidate members of the House through the language he was using. The question I asked was a legitimate one and the parliamentary secretary's language was disparaging. He used unparliamentary language when he described my question, both in the adjournment debate and previously, as demogoguery. If you, Madam Speaker, would check Beau-chesne's, you would find that this is definitely unparliamentary language.
I call on the hon. member to withdraw his statement and to desist from trying to intimidate members, thereby stifling debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis Duclos (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MR. FRIESEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. DUCLOS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I remember very well the exchange that the hon. member and myself had on the evening in question. 1 must say that I did not want to offend him. It seems to me that, during that particular debate, both the hon. member and several of his colleagues of the official opposition took unfair advantage of the little knowledge that most citizens have about the scope of the protocol of agreement between the Soviet Union and Canada. I believe that it was really unfair of the hon. member and some of his colleagues to suggest that, under this protocol, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could have transmitted to the Soviet Union what are for all practical purposes state secrets, namely the results of conversations between representatives of the Canadian government and of other countries belonging to the Atlantic Alliance.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-625, to amend the Criminal Code (power to take blood samples).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the purpose of my bill is to correct what I perceive to be a weakness in the law as it applies to the problem of drinking and driving. The purpose of this bill is to allow for the testing of blood samples for blood alcohol levels in cases where, because of injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident, drivers are not now subject to testing when suspected of impaired driving.
I bring this bill forward because at a highway intersection not far from where I live there was a collision of automobiles and a young man, whose life was full of potential and promise, was killed. The person driving the other vehicle in this case was suspected of being extremely intoxicated, according to several witnesses. Unfortunately, because of the existing law, no blood level testing could be conducted. Within several days that same person, that driver whose drinking and driving had just brought about the tragic death, was again on the road.
Therefore I want to assure the House that in my proposed amendment to the Criminal Code authority would only be given and exercised in the event that breathalyzer testing is not feasible and securing a blood sample does not interfere with any form of medical treatment.
It is time to close this simple gap now. I urge that this bill be accepted for first, second, and third readings.

subsubtopic: DALHOUSIE-BELLEDUNE PORT STUDY
speechtext: The Dalhousie-Belledune Port study was commissioned jointly by the province of New Brunswick and DREE in mid-1979 to determine future potential of the public harbour of Dalhousie and the NHB Port of Beiledune. The study was awarded to ADI Limited, Fredericton, N.B., who submitted an initial progress report in December, 1979, and a second progress report in April, 1980. In August, 1980, the steering committee for the study, under the chairmanship of the province, approved a request from the consultant to postpone completion of the study and preparation of a final report pending the availability of important environmental and economic information relevant to the Belledune-Dalhousie study. The information to which the consultant made reference is the subject of separate studies for which final reports are not anticipated before November of this year. In light of this it is not anticipated that the Dalhousie-Belledune study will be completed before some time in the new year. With regard to the release of the study following its completion, provincial representatives have not yet indicated if they wish to make the final report public.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its incompetent housing policies, which have led directly to soaring housing costs, plummeting housing starts, and critically low vacancy rates.
He said: Madam Speaker, we have proposed this motion to the House because we are concerned about the state of affairs in the housing sector in Canada. Housing costs have soared to a point where it is difficult for present home owners to maintain their homes and almost impossible for first-time home owners to purchase homes. Housing starts have plummeted, reflecting a state of concern in an industry which employs hundreds of thousands of Canadians and indicating social problems now and in the future. Vacancy rates have reached low points in many areas across Canada, indicating that Canadians are having difficulty finding places to live.
Because we want to air the question completely, to propose solutions and to spur the government on to action, we have proposed the following motion:
That this House condemns the government for its incompetent housing policies, which have led directly to soaring housing costs, plummeting housing starts, and critically low vacancy rates.
There is no speech dealing with the crisis facing the housing sector today which would be complete without reference to the crippling mortgage interest rates facing Canadians. I would not for a minute suggest that the Liberal government has completely ignored this crisis faced by hundreds of thousands of Canadian families who are renewing their mortgages. For example, before he was appointed to cabinet, on March 2, 1980, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) promised that "mortgage interest will be the issue the new government will give priority". Ten months later it has received as much priority as his industrial strategy.
January 14, 1981

The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) promised to look at the impact upon home owners and potential home owners of interest rates, to see what special steps could be taken. Not to be outdone, the minister responsible for housing promised on November 7,
1980,	to watch the situation. On November 13, 1980, he reiterated strongly, "We are watching the situation", and on December 15, 1980, he was "meeting" and "visiting." The fact remains that despite criminally high mortgage interest rates, the government has done nothing to cushion the impact of today's 15.5 per cent mortgage interest rates upon home owners who were paying 10.5 per cent in 1976 and must renew their five-year mortgages in 1981.
The government has moved to help the unfortunate victims of the Liberal AHOP program, and well it should. The AHOP program was a potential disaster for every mortgage that was put out, and every real estate sales person and lawyer practising real estate law in Canada knew it. The only ones who were fooled were CMHC and the Liberal government.
Putting that fact aside, I want to ask the government about what happened to universality. Canada has adopted the theory of universality from baby bonus to old age security programs. Why is the Liberal government abandoning that theory when it comes to mortgages? Why does it refuse to recognize the hardships which today's mortgage interest rates are putting on the Canadian family?
Not only does the government fail to recognize the hardships faced by Canadians who are paying outrageous mortgage interest rates, it also stands by while innocent Canadians who have not accepted government assistance such as AHOP or have not defaulted on CMHC guaranteed mortgages are in positions where they can be sued on the covenant to pay.
The House will know that a mortgage is security for a debt. If the Government of Canada honours its guarantees on the government-insured mortgages, or takes over the AHOP mortgages, and its policy is not to sue the former owner for any deficiency between the recovery on sale and the amount guaranteed and paid out by the government, we all know that the institutional lenders do not have to be as generous and they are entitled to sue. That is why we are concerned about Canadian home owners today.
A Canadian home owner renewing a $50,000 mortgage in
1981,	which was taken out in 1976 at 10'/2 per cent, is faced today with a 15'/2 per cent mortgage interest rate. That can mean as much as $177 a month in additional carrying charges. So, why do we discriminate against the Canadian who is trying to carry that mortgage? Despite posturing, promises and postponements, the Liberal party is refusing to assist the average Canadian to overcome that burden.
The New Democratic Party joined with their Liberal counterparts to condemn our party when we brought in our mortgage interest and realty tax credit plan. Let us see what that alternative would have done for the Canadian home owner. Based upon a $33,000 mortgage at today's Liberal interest
Housing
rate of 15'/2 per cent, a Canadian family would have been entitled to a tax credit of $1,125 a year, or $94 a month. That $94 a month would go a long way toward offsetting the mortgage interest rates which the government is fostering and condoning. Our party wants to make home ownership more affordable for Canadians.
The Liberal party criticized our plan. During the last election it was suggested that the 18-cent federal excise tax was to be used to subsidize our program. 1 challenge the minister responsible for housing, who will hopefully enter this debate. The government has increased the excise tax on gasoline, and it has increased the cost of gasoline. Ministers have produced an unheard of tax on home heating oil, as well as increasing the deficit by $3 billion. Given those increases, how can they account for the fact that they have increased the hardships which are facing Canadian home owners without assisting them in any way whatsoever? If they criticized us for proposing to tax Canadians and return some of the tax money to those who need it, how can they justify taxing Canadians, increasing the cost of gasoline and the deficit, and doing nothing to help home owners?
The government has increased the cost of gasoline to the consumer. It has increased the taxes on gasoline, home heating oil and natural gas. We proposed an energy tax credit. That was a tax credit of $220 for the average Canadian family earning under $21,380 per year. It would have lowered the cost burden for the low-income family, which now exists under the Liberal government scheme. We appeal to the government to alleviate the unjust burden which now rests on the low and middle-income earners by introducing a similar energy tax credit.
We are concerned about the level of housing starts in the country. Traditionally, a review of housing starts serves two purposes. It indicates the level of activity in the housing sector of the economy. Jobs in the construction industry and related industries depend upon this activity. Construction workers, forestry workers, real estate salespersons and retail outlet clerks at hardware stores, to name a few, are people who depend directly or indirectly on activity in the housing sector for their livelihood. Banks and investment houses review their loan and investment portfolios with an eye to the health of the housing industry. Just as important to Canadians, we use housing starts to gauge how well we are moving toward our goal of placing every Canadian in a decent, affordable housing situation in a sound community environment. As either an economic indicator or a social gauge, Canadians have cause to be concerned about the incompetent housing policies of this government which have led to the lowest level of housing starts in years.
Figures provided by CMHC confirm that the lack of government policy in the housing field is seriously widening the gap between the number of housing starts CMHC says is necessary to house Canadians adequately and the number of housing starts which actually take place. In 1980 alone it was estimated by CMHC that we required 266,000 housing starts. The government produced 160,000 housing starts. For the past

January 14, 1981
Housing
four years we have failed miserably to meet those goals. Our average requirements were 260,000 housing starts, but the Liberal government only achieved 209,000. But most important is the fact that it is getting worse. The shortfall in 1980 means we only achieved 60 per cent of our target.
Our vacancy rates indicate that Canadians are having difficulties finding adequate accommodation in many areas. First-time home owners are finding it impossible to finance a home in some areas, and difficult to find one in other areas. The government has consistently failed to produce policy or programs which will have a significant impact on housing starts. Housing shortages, rising prices and the lack of activity, all demand in decency that the government initiate some action.
Home ownership is part of the Canadian dream, whether you are a first, fifth or tenth generation Canadian. Traditionally, Canadian couples saved to own a home. Because of the lack of action by this government that dream is turning into a nightmare.
There was a study produced by the University of Guelph which stated that the question is not: how and when can we afford a house? Rather, it is: can we have a satisfying life without a house, a garden and a mortgage? 1 am prepared to admit that there are many times when I can do without a garden. I can definitely manage without a mortgage all the time.
Let us look at that dream. The study points out that a modestly-priced family home costs $70,000 in Canada. With a 10 per cent down payment a buyer is faced with a $63,000 mortgage to carry that house. At today's rate of \5Vi per cent the monthly mortgage payments would be $679.75. The study goes on to point out the other escalating costs which are a direct result of action, or inaction, by the government, including heating, insurance and transportation. The home is a traditional foundation for a strong family life. I ask the minister when will the government act to assist Canadians to buy a home and achieve the Canadian dream?
The reduction in housing starts has had a negative effect upon employment in the housing sector. The Canadian Construction Association estimates an employment multiplier effect of 1.25 to 1.75 jobs per housing start. The 1980 shortfall alone of 106,000 housing starts represents a loss to the Canadian economy of between 132,000 and 176,000 jobs. There are
95,000	Canadians who want to be employed in the construction industry, that is 14.3 per cent of the work force which is unemployed. Since this government took office as much as 21.7 per cent of the work force engaged in construction has been out of work.
This decline points out a long-term problem which I would ask government ministers to address themselves to now, so that when recovery comes we will be ready. As employment opportunities decrease in the housing sector there are skilled workers who are tempted to leave for other industries with more stability. They take their skills with them. When we return to the level of activity which is acceptable in the housing industry, with the level where it should be, they will be reluctant to
return. I ask the minister what provision is he making to find an adequate supply of labour, if and when he ever will assist the housing industry to recover? The supply of skilled labour is vital to that recovery.
In view of the social and economic impact which housing starts have, let us be fair and review what little action the government has taken. The only initiatives of any significance in the field of housing starts are the reintroduction of the Multiple Unit Residential Building program and the provision of additional funding under the National Housing Act social housing programs.
Experts have already predicted that the high interest rates will offset the tax benefits of the MURB program. The increase in funding for 5,000 units under non-profit and co-operative housing programs is commendable, but one cannot help but wonder when studying the long-range results. I am concerned that the same situation may arise as with the AHOP program when the developments begin to age and extensive repairs and renovations are required. A study should be undertaken to find out what will happen down the road. Let us look at the situation now, not when the problems begin. In the long run, social assistance to individuals by way of a shelter allowance may make a lot more sense than financial assistance to bricks and mortar.
It is estimated by the Progressive Conservative Party that its mortgage interest and realty tax credit program would have increased the level of housing starts by 20,000 to 35,000 ownership units annually. We are not saying that it is the answer, but it is an alternative and it would have worked for four to five years. It would have had the social effect of increasing the supply of homes and making them more affordable for Canadians. Using the multiplier effect of 1.5 jobs per housing start, the program alone would have created 30,000 to
50,000	jobs annually for that same four-year to five-year period.
The biggest criticism of our program by the Liberal party was a silent admission that it had no program which even remotely compared with ours. That party did not have a program then and it does not have a program now. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), who is responsible for housing, is presiding over one of the most disastrous periods in the history of the housing industry in Canada. His answer to the chaos surrounding him, when he is questioned in this House is, "We are monitoring the situation." Surely, the time has come for action rather than reflection. We urge the minister to swallow his pride and adopt the Progressive Conservative mortgage interest plan and, failing that, we urge him to take more forceful action to stimulate housing starts in Canada.
I would like to refer briefly to the Community Services Contribution Program because it affects the housing sector. The government has demonstrated very little concern for either the serious economic and employment problems of Canada or agreements reached with the provinces. On Novem-
January 14, 1981

ber 12, 1980, the minister of housing announced in this House the cancellation of the Community Services Contribution Program. The global agreement between the provinces and the federal government which his predecessor signed specifically states:
Canada and the province(s) agree that prior to December 31, 1980, they will endeavour to replace the agreement with a new agreement that provides a long-term certainty to the community services program.
The only long-term certainty they received was that the program no longer exists. Either the minister of housing does not take much stock in agreements or he just does not have the clout to represent the home owners of Canada and the municipalities of this country in cabinet. On July 10, 1980, in reply to a question in this House the minister stated:
I have recommended to the officials of the corporation and to the government that, because of the time of year, the program be extended for at least one year.
That promise was made again on October 11, 1980, when the minister spoke to the Newfoundland and Labrador Federation of Municipalities. Three days later in this House, on October 14, 1980, the minister stated if the program could not be continued, "that some other way will be found to assist the municipalities". The government, Mr. Speaker, entered into a written agreement which it then ignored. The minister gave assurances both inside and outside this House about extensions and alternate programs, all of which have been ignored. I would ask the minister how can the provinces and the municipalities continue to deal with him when his word is being broken?
I have another suggestion which the minister may like to consider. When the program was cancelled, the minister stated that it was cancelled because 50 per cent of the money went to soft services such as recreation services. I have the figures here and, in fact, only 11.4 per cent went to soft services in 1979, and in 1980 the portion was 7 per cent. These figures were prepared by CMHC. 1 hesitate to suggest that the minister misled the House, but either he did not have the figures in front of him or perhaps he ought to take another look at the term "soft services".

speechtext:
We are concerned about the cancellation of this program for two reasons. The first reason is that the Government of Canada broke its word on the agreement and to the municipalities. The second reason is that the cancellation concerns employment. A large proportion of that employment was in the hard services area of the construction industry- sewers, water, storm sewers and so on. The government has cast aside the economic, employment and social benefits which would accrue to a great number of Canadians through the program.
I do not believe that the government had any business in the field in the first place. The power and responsibility for that kind of servicing belong, in my opinion, to the provinces, but once it is in the field and after having led people down the garden path through agreements, surely the government has the responsibility to withdraw in an orderly fashion. We urge
Housing
the government to reintroduce the Community Services Contribution Program in such a way that proper consideration is given to the projects which municipalities had under way at the time the government cancelled the program.
When the home insulation program was introduced in 1977, one of the major objectives was to save energy used for space heating by stimulating action on the part of individual Canadians to upgrade the thermal efficiency of existing housing stock. We support that objective. "The National Energy Program", which was really the budget introduced on October 28, 1980, further elaborated on this objective. It stated: "Improving the energy efficiency of existing housing makes good sense. It must proceed faster than it has." We support that statement.
The government's answer to these high-sounding, philosophical promises was to increase the CHIP budget from $80 million per year to $265 million per year. Period. Stop there. No further. There is no mention about the three million Canadian homes built after 1961 which are not eligible under CHIP even though their insulation standards were much the same. There was no mention of expanding the CHIP program to include other materials such as double glazed and triple glazed windows. These help to save heat and energy, and are an essential part of proper home insulation. It is only common sense that we use every possible tactic to save energy, and windows and doors must be considered when insulating homes.
What we are asking of the government is that it immediately extend the CHIP program so that the three million homes built after 1961 and before September 1, 1977, can be properly insulated, and that it expand the program to include hermetically sealed windows, thermal pane windows and doors in order to achieve optimum efficiency from energy saving.
I would like to talk a bit about vacancy rates, which are mentioned at the tale end of the motion. It is serious to suggest that Canadians are finding difficulty in maintaining their standard of shelter, but it is even more serious to have a situation where Canadians cannot even find a place to live. CMHC vacancy rates indicate that Canadians are indeed having a difficult time finding a place to live, due to a lack of action by the government. In the two-year period, from October, 1978, to October, 1980, the national average for vacancy rates fell from an acceptable rate of 4.6 per cent to the critical and unacceptable rate of an average of 2.3 per cent.
This problem stretches from coast to coast. In Victoria the rate is .1 per cent; in Saskatoon, .6 per cent; in Toronto, .6 per cent, and in St. John's, Newfoundland, it is .1 per cent. As I mentioned earlier, experts suggest that the rising interest rates have cancelled the benefits of the MURB program.
As a token stimulus to provide low rental housing, the minister announced on June 17, 1980, funding for 5,000 additional non-profit housing units. In the same statement he noted and admitted that between 1977 and 1979, rental housing approvals dropped by 54,000. That is a drop in the bucket provided for low rental housing. In fact, in 1980 the CMHC figures indicate that multiple housing starts were down by 36 per cent compared with 1979. Clearly we need to see some
6200

January 14, 1981
Housing
dramatic action by this government and this minister to correct what is fast becoming a national disaster.
Earlier, I dealt briefly with the subject of shelter allowances, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest to the minister that he seriously consider introducing a shelter allowance program. There are some advantages to this. It is a direct cash payment to the individual and is subject to income requirements. It does not go toward bricks and mortar so we would not find ourselves tied up with buildings across the country. It would also give families a choice of where to live and how to live. They could carry the benefits from household to household and from place to place. There are other benefits as well. Owners of rental units could charge more realistic rents without harmful effect to the tenants. Most important, of course, is that it would encourage builders to build rental units.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we are very, very concerned about the critical state of the housing sector in Canada today. We believe this has been caused by the action and inaction, mostly inaction, of the government. We have outlined the problems and suggested some solutions because we feel that Canadians deserve a better opportunity to have decent, affordable housing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is delightful to hear my Tory colleagues castigate the present government for incompetent housing policies. Of course 1 agree with them, yet in 1979 the Conservatives offered no housing programs for average and low-income Canadians, no means that I know of for young couples to get into home ownership, no relief for tenants, and their mortgage tax credit benefit program would have benefited only those who were lucky enough to already be in homes and not those in the greatest need. I would hardly call that a "universal program," to quote my colleague.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker, we agree with the motion put forward by the Conservative party today. The Liberal government has no effective policy and few effective programs to deal with the housing crisis that now affects most Canadians. It does, however, have a very effective economic policy to ensure that young couples will never get into home ownership. High interest rates have caused home owners to lose their homes. The government and the minister responsible for CMHC have no social goals, no over-all, comprehensive goals for a social housing policy for Canada and, therefore, no comprehensive planning to deal with the housing needs of the country.
We agree that rents are extremely high. In seven major Canadian cities there is a zero vacancy rate and in those cities in particular rents are astronomical. The cost of new housing is extremely high in all parts of Canada, and particularly in
those parts where there is economic growth it has risen out of the reach of most Canadians.
I think the Liberals are great dabblers, Mr. Speaker. As my colleague pointed out, they give programs with one hand and take them away with the other. Perhaps that keeps ministers and bureaucrats employed.
The Neighbourhood Improvement Program was successful and involved communities in rehabilitating their neighbourhoods, but it was taken away. Now the government has cancelled Community Service Contribution Programs to municipalities, the very programs and grants that are essential if municipalities are to control land, service land, and make it available for affordable housing.
Instead of providing for smaller, integrated public housing a few years ago when the housing act was changed, the government did away with public housing altogether. Ministers did not seem to realize that there are poor people in the country. There is no single federal program now that deals with 100 per cent poverty communities.
According to some examples that I will come to later, the Liberals apparently believe that what goes on in remote areas of Canada and is not seen by those of us who sit in this House, is of little concern to ordinary Canadians. I submit that is not so. Last December I learned that $20 million had been arbitrarily cut from the budget for native housing. This is an immoral act, Mr. Speaker, when we know that over 50 per cent of the homes of Indian people on reserves are practically just shacks. They have no running water, little sanitation, and this poor housing is contributing to genocide. The government is directly responsible for this. The government must increase the budget for native housing just to catch up with its broken promises and accumulated neglect of years past.
I was very shocked to learn that RRAP, the home repair program instigated in the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and sponsored by the National Anti Poverty Organization, was arbitrarily terminated the day before yesterday. The NAPO group was informed yesterday. From my observation this program was very successful and had rehabilitated some 200 homes in fishing villages, and indeed had rehabilitated whole villages like Parson's Pond. It is a program that seems to be pretty unique and is the best antidote to protecting poor people and those who just have minimum employment each year, from inflation. Some unemployed people own their own homes. They do not have mortgages and they put their own labour into repairs. It is an economic, sound program from any point of view, yet it was arbitrarily cancelled without consultation with the local communities much less with the 100 or more people who had applied for assistance for home repairs and had expected to start on them this winter.
I cannot blame the minister responsible for CMHC alone for many of the dilemmas and for the poor housing policy in this country. Last Monday I pleaded with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to take emergency action in face of the housing crisis that is hurting the country, largely because of his economic policy and the very high and fluctuating interest rates. I tried to make him see that young couples are
January 14, 1981

unable to plan for families because they will never own a home. Later he said, "Of course, you know that there is a decreasing family formation in Canada.", implying that we did not need more housing, when in fact he is the very one that is causing this decrease inthe birth rate.
In many cities it is common for tenants to pay over 50 per cent of their income for rent. Home owners are faced with mortgage interest rates of 16 per cent and higher, and indeed some people will never own a home. The minister did not seem willing to admit this. Of course we know of many homeless students, particularly in the lower mainland of British Columbia, who slept in cars last fall. I presume they are now crashing in pads with their friends. What way is this for young people to get on with their training for future opportunities? The minister ignored these problems just as he ignored my request for major increase in funds for affordable, non-profit housing. It is the only program which can make a great impact on the present situation.
Everyone knows, of course, that the cost of accommodation today is astronomical. Home costs and rents are completely out of control. Prices are escalating far more rapidly than the rate of inflation, with no real relationship to the value of a particular home. For example, my husband and I bought a modest bungalow on a 33-foot lot in Vancouver East some 20 years ago. We paid $9,000 for it.

Yes, we were lucky to be in a home. Today that house would sell for about $150,000. If we waited until next week to sell it, chances are very good that it would be worth $160,000. If I were looking for a home today in my riding, or in most parts of Canada, I would be faced with interest rates over 16 per cent for short-term mortgages. This means people must find close to $1,000 for monthly costs including house payments, fuel and taxes. No one earning under $35,000 per annum, including members of Parliament if they did not have a home, can get into a first home today at these rates.
Many of the immigrants in my riding are getting homes by banding together with not two but at least three wage earners sharing costs of payment. Chances are they will never pay off the full cost of their home in their lifetimes. This leads to drastic overcrowding and a living standard which most of us would not agree is warranted in a country like Canada.
My colleague talked at length about AHOP, as I have in the past, so I will not dwell on that. I understand people who have bought homes under AHOP are holding a meeting tonight in an Ottawa suburb. These people will be losing their homes because they cannot renew their mortgages at the escalated rates, a problem to which the very unrealistic policy of AHOP contributed.
We in the NDP have advocated a mortgage assistance plan for some years now. Recently I proposed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that over $1 billion of the profits which
Housing
Canadian banks have accumulated as a result of the fluctuating interest rates caused by the Minister of Finance and the government, should be set aside in a special fund. This could be a fund for a lending portfolio which would offer stable lower-interest mortgages, particularly for young people who are trying to get into a first home. As we know, the Prime Minister ignored this suggestion.
The Minister of Finance actually has the power to request a fund like this of the banks. It has been done in the past. It was done in the days when we had 30-year mortgages at a set rate of, I believe, 6 per cent. It worked well. This request has not been considered, except I noticed the minister responsible for CMHC had a glint in his eye when I mentioned $1 billion.
I have said many times in this House that the MURB tax write-off is a useless program and we should get rid of it. It is not being used anyway because interest rates are too high. Let us put the $15 million which the government was going to be willing to sacrifice in tax write-offs into funds for affordable housing, and let us up the amount from there.
The programs of the government are inadequate, of course, because they treat shelter not as a social necessity and a right of Canadians. The government treats these programs really as a method of manipulating or trying to manipulate the economic system. This is wrong. Housing, just like medicare and old age pensions and many other social programs which we now realize are essential in a country like Canada, is a right and a necessity. It must be affordable and available to all Canadians. This must be the basic philosophy but it is not the philosophy of either the Liberals or the Conservatives. The free enterprise parties say every day "leave it to the private sector". That is why we have the mess we have now in the whole area of housing. We left it to the private sector. 1 tell the hon. member from Vancouver to have a look at who is doing the speculating if he does not believe me.
We need long-range planning, Mr. Speaker. But we need a decent sound policy to start with. We need planning for housing based on population trends, on immigration policies, and on geographic concentrations of growth where we know there is potential for more jobs and where more workers will go. If the government brings in 50,000 refugees, then the government should provide-it did not-extra housing in the areas where these people are going to settle. Why should low-income Canadians be pushed out of affordable low-rent housing because of our immigration policies? It is not fair to either the immigrants or to the Canadians, who are likely to express a good deal of dissent.
I have said that most tenants now pay far in excess of 30 per cent of their incomes on rent. In a study done in Vancouver those who pay over 60 per cent of their incomes are predominantly senior citizens, single parents, lonely women who are in the high percentage of people in poverty, and native Indians. Does this seem like a just society, even to Liberals and Conservatives?
I ask the minister responsible for CMHC to look into the whole question of excessive speculation which is also causing housing prices to shoot sky high. I do not have the time to go

January 14, 1981
Housing
into this in depth, but foreign ownership in Vancouver is also a major contributing factor to this problem. We feel some action must be taken on the question of capital gains tax to discourage excessive speculation on homes which are not the primary or first home of a family.

speechtext: They are already taxed.

speechtext:
Since my time is almost up, I would like to summarize ten recommendations which I hope the government will consider for action to help alleviate the housing crisis in Canada.
First, let us recognize the problem at least, and make housing a top priority for government action immediately. I know we have to convince the cabinet as a whole that this is essential.
Second, call an emergency conference which will include provincial representatives, municipal representatives, non-profit societies, tenants and co-operatives-people who know what the housing crisis is all about first-hand. It is not surprising that in March the minister is supporting a real estate conference which is to bring together developers and real estate interests again. Yet there are no funds provided for tenants and home owners and private groups to attend, and these are the people who know from a consumer point of view what is needed.
Third, the government should instigate a mortgage assistance program in co-operation with the banks to reduce mortgage interest rates to new home owners, particularly those earning less than $35,000 a year.
Fourth, provide federal Crown land and provincial Crown land, loans, grants and land banking incentives to try to get more land reserved and leased, if possible, for co-operative and other forms of affordable housing. I would like to see a buy-back clause built into these programs so that there will not be exploitation and profit-making on these kinds of subsidized programs and they will be useful for future generations.
Fifth, let us control housing speculation with an increase in capital gains tax to 100 per cent for resale of homes and real estate which are not the primary residence. Let us have sell-back clauses for all government subsidized housing programs.
Sixth, let us improve housing for tenants by encouraging provincial rent controls and shelter allowances, especially for tenants with special needs. We need to increase the budget for non-profit housing. In the Bob Rae budget last summer we proposed a housing investment which would provide rotating funds of up to $500 million. We would continue to advocate this.
Seventh, let us continue to expand the RRAP programs. I commend the minister for improving the guidelines for this program. However, we should expand it, make it more flexible, more adaptable and community based for rural areas, areas like the one I mentioned in Newfoundland.
The CHIP program and insulation programs need to be improved and made available for newer houses. We need to be assured that insulation will be safe and not dangerous to health.
My ninth recommendation is to increase research and development funds in order to develop energy efficient, affordable housing, particularly modular prefabricated housing manufactured in Canada, creating an industry for Canadians. There are many other innovative housing ideas for which research and development funds should be allocated.
Any federal government program or federal funds which go into local programs such as rapid transit should take into account that land is reserved for non-profit affordable housing. For example, in the greater Vancouver region the federal government will be giving assistance to a rapid transit system. We should act now to ensure that areas near the rapid transit depots will be available for lower cost housing for those who cannot afford to live in the centre of the city.
Finally, our party supports this motion put forward by the Conservatives. We agree that housing requires emergency action. The present government is doing little to recognize and even less to alleviate this problem. Canadians deserve better and more affordable housing. Housing is a human right and should be written into our constitution. The government must take action and do it now.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning I wish to congratulate both members who have spoken this afternoon, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell). In their comments they offered alternative suggestions and specific proposals which they urged the government to consider or adopt in order to address what they perceive to be a crisis in housing. I hope, that when I have concluded my comments, I will have touched on some of the specific points raised and hit upon some of these matters. As I say, it is encouraging that they offered alternatives. While my comments may show that I disagree in policy, nonetheless it is encouraging to have heard these constructive comments.
As the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I am aware of the housing problems in this country today. Part of the problem, of course, as identified, is the reduction or decline in housing production which has created a severe shortage in some parts of Canada. However, I would like to point out that there are encouraging signs. The trough has been reached and the upturn has begun. I am encouraged in that by the Conference Board in Canada.
Their forecast shows starts for next year up by some 20,000 over this year, to approximately 181,000 units. That is an encouraging sign. The 160,000 starts this year is remarkable notwithstanding the high interest rates, the change in government, the fact that industry looks to government for leadership and there was some halting in the industry. Nothwithstanding those facts, we have seen a strong number of starts of approximately 160,000 units.
January 14, 1981

In my view, the recovery at this time relates to the government's approach, which is to say that the private sector, rather than massive government intervention, should act in this market so as to obviate distortions which have occurred in the past. Hon. members will recall better than I that the federal government was required to intervene in the marketplace in the early years of the previous decade. This resulted in a production boom, and subsequently, after 1975, overproduction. That contributed to a downturn in the industry. A more reasonable recovery is occurring this time based on the operation of normal market conditions. I conclude that this will lead to a greater stability in the industry in years to come.
I will return to the current situation a little later. In the meantime, I believe it would be appropriate to set the record straight on the mandate of the federal government and its role through CMHC as an agency of government, and on the accomplishments of the government and the corporation over the years.
Social and economic changes in Canada during the past three and a half decades have increasingly required CMHC to take on a new and more comprehensive role in the fields of housing and community services. I notice that there is at least one member of the House, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has the advantage over all of us of having watched that occur from the perspective of a member of this House. I am happy he is here today during this debate.
