speechtext:
It would take the better part of the afternoon to give a picture of CMHC's development over the years, so I will limit my references to a few of the milestones. Essentially I am talking about the development of CMHC, first as a financial institution and, second, as an agency of the federal government in administering social housing policies.
Its initial mandate, and I am talking about the financial aspect, was to cause more housing to be built to meet immediate and urgent needs. That was met by CMHC within the first few years, using a variety of supportive measures. I think of joint loans with banks, buy-back guarantees, rental guarantees for a minimum return, and the like.
In its social housing role the first major milestone was reached in 1949 when the National Housing Act was broadened to include a housing program. This program, a shared cost partnership arrangement with the provinces, subsequently became one of the most important features of Canadian housing legislation. It led eventually to such programs as non-profit and co-operative housing programs, touched upon today by previous speakers, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, rural and native housing and a number of other programs.
In its role as a financial institution, CMHC introduced mortgage insurance in 1954 as one of the most useful ways of meeting Canadian housing needs. The objective was to attract private funding into the industry, and that was an immensely successful move by the government.
Housing
Mortgage insurance rapidly became the main instrument of the government policy. On the supply side, in the same year, 1954, the Bank Act was amended to allow the chartered banks to make mortgage loans. These financial initiatives encouraged home buying and gave additional impetus to the construction industry. In the late 1960s, mortgage investment was made even more attractive by two further changes, the introduction of the five-year mortgage term and the removal of interest ceilings on bank loans.
I would like to emphasize that the purpose of NHA mortgage insurance is primarily to increase the flow of private capital into the housing sector of the economy. At the same time, by means of inspection services, mortgage insurance has allowed CMHC to exert a continuing influence on the quality and kind of housing built in Canada.
The outstanding results of the mortgage insurance program can be summarized quickly. Of the five million dwellings completed since 1954 in Canada, a full 40 per cent have been insured by CMHC. This has entailed some $36 billion in capital funds that have been attracted towards investment in new housing under the program. CMHC has also insured $12 billion on mortgages on existing dwellings.
All of this housing has been required to conform to the CMHC standards about which I have spoken. I think that by any measurement NHA insurance has been an outstanding success in meeting the objective of attracting private funds into the market to create a stable environment for the investment of private funding and in the establishment of quality criteria in the construction of housing.
As an instrument of social policy, beginning in 1950 CMHC developed even more broadly. The whole community rather than individual homes became the focus of the corporation's drive. Contrary to some comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, this has been an objective and a policy, and the corporation has a record of success in addressing this area of concern of the government, social housing. Between 1955 and 1963, for example, urban renewal was a major consideration. In later years CMHC's involvement in the community extended to assistance for sewage and water services, and to the provision of social amenities.
My statistics show that one of every four members of this House has served in elected office at the local level, and I doubt if any of those members would question the usefulness of the role of CMHC through that period of time.
During this period and into the sixties the provincial governments became more active in housing and community planning, and the NHA amendments in 1964 responded to this trend. This was new to most provinces. However, arrangements were thus made with the provinces for the joint financing of public housing and as well for a wider range of urban renewal projects.
The bulldozing techniques originally hit upon were replaced some ten years later with programs to conserve and rehabilitate. They have been touched upon. After 1969 the main

January 14, 1981
Housing
thrust of the federal support was toward housing which served people in the lower income brackets, as CME1C became recognized as an instrument of social as well as economic policy of the government.
A number of programs were introduced to encourage the production of moderately-priced homes for rental and ownership. Low interest loans and subsidies greatly assisted in the production of low rental housing by non-profit and co-operative organizations as well as private interests. These measures helped many thousands of Canadian families to obtain housing either as owners or tenants which they could not otherwise have attained. It is true that some people, because of economic conditions, have met difficulties under some of the programs, but by far the majority of these families continue to enjoy their homes and reasonable financial security.
The volatile housing market of the seventies, with its demand for housing, its accelerating prices and the tight rental market, put a considerable strain on federal funds. This resulted, first, in combining private financing on some programs with federal subsidies and, later, with a whole new approach to federal financing. I refer here to the graduated payment mortgage, for example, which was introduced to take the pressure off the federal subsidy program by providing easier pay-back arrangements during the first few difficult years of a loan.
Substantial changes were made in CMHC's social housing program, as hon. members know. The new approach provided for private financing of social housing projects sponsored by private non-profit agencies with enriched federal subsidies through interest write-downs and full protection to lenders through mortgage insurance. This was a device by which the government, in conjunction with the private sector, combined, to provide more housing than otherwise would have been provided for people in low-income categories who were finding it difficult to compete in the private market. That, if I need remind the hon. member for Vancouver East, was the basis for the policy of the government of engaging with the private sector in this type of arrangement.
The federal government is well aware of the problems faced by some home owners who have renewed or are renewing their mortgages at high interest rates. The effects of these rates, 1 submit, however, are not as serious as has sometimes been reported. Only a small minority of home owners face dire hardship as a result of high rates.
In the vast majority of instances incomes will have increased enough during the past five years or so to offset the increase in mortgage payments. Last year about 350,000 home owners renewed their mortgages. This year that number will probably be about half a million, partly because some 100,000 home owners took out one-year mortgages last year. Naturally, the incidence of home owners who experience difficulty in meeting their monthly payments after renewal will depend upon the prevailing interest rate. As we have observed, the interest rate has moderated during the last month, and it is our expectation-and 1 am optimistic-that the rate will continue in a
downward trend to such a level that home owners renewing will find it acceptable.
In the case of homes bought under AHOP, touched upon by the hon. member for Simcoe North, we said in 1975 at the initiation of the program that if any home owners found themselves in an untenable position at the end of the initial five-year period, the government would provide or consider further assistance. We are meeting that pledge. We moved in March of last year by making contributions to families which purchased under this plan and which encountered unexpected hardship to provide assistance, which was intended to reduce monthly mortgage and tax payments where possible to a maximum of 30 per cent of a family's income.
When Parliament opened last April we announced that we planned to help home owners who might lose their homes as a result of higher monthly payments resulting from higher interest rates but, as I said, the interest rate spiral has moderated. A few weeks ago when concern was increasing we took a look at the plans we had adopted in May, but the moderation has saved us from that course of action.
Our policy, as 1 indicated earlier, is to intervene in the marketplace when it is not functioning properly and when serious needs are identified. For example, last year, as already touched on, we moved to increase by 5,000 units the social housing starts and units subsidized by the federal government. Neither member who has spoken this afternoon has indicated that that is 5,000 on top of an annual number of 25,000. Hon. members who say we are not addressing the housing needs of people in low and moderate-income brackets should add that
5,000	to that 25,000, put the result beside the total number of starts for the year of 160,000 and consider the cost to the taxpayer. In my opinion that is a substantial and continuing response to that problem.
Incidentally, Vancouver was one of the cities where this assistance was required. We initially approved 892 units of social housing under this initiative for the greater Vancouver area. We discovered before long that with a vacancy rate of .4 further action was required. As a result, a month ago we approved an additional 800 units to help meet this critical shortage.
As hon. members know and have touched upon, in the budget the minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) reintroduced MURB assistance. It has been suggested that the starts which are generated by that will not be picked up by the private sector. My information from the private sector is to the contrary, and I have seen in announcements from the province of British Columbia through its minister of housing, and the minister responsible for housing in the province of Ontario, that both those provincial governments are considering an add-on to that initiative by the federal government so that we can address jointly again the question of the housing needs of low or moderate income Canadians in those areas where we all recognize that there has been a shift and the markets are tight, especially in the rental market area.
I would like to turn to another matter which bears mentioning. Shortly after the Conservatives formed the government in
January 14, 1981

1979, they turned their attention to the possibility of privatizing some or all of CMHC. We know that this proposal resulted in the document known as the Matthews report, which has received considerable publicity.
Many people were led to believe, and I think incorrectly, that CMHC was beset by serious problems which threatened its doom. The interesting thing to me is that in the Matthews report those provisions which addressed the issues were not referred to. For example a passage in the report reads:
A very significant factor in the outlook for the eighties is the enormous past accomplishments of the housing industry, the financial industry, and government. Together these groups have produced a virtually unsurpassed stock of housing for Canadians, with almost no significant pool of unsatisfied housing requirements.
It seems to me that what is being said here-and I address the point-is that the CMHC has helped to do a good job. To argue that because it has done a good job, it should cease its operations-1 think the implication in the report was that CMHC was not required any further-does not make sense. If CMHC has done a great job, which is my experience in the ministry-its expertise and its reputation for concern in housing, not only in the financial sense but in the social sense are known-the argument is all the stronger for ensuring that it continue to be a valuable instrument to the government and to Canadians as we address the question of housing in the 1980s.
Reference has been made to the mortgage deductibility plan of the official opposition. The hon. member for Simcoe North did not say that it addressed home owners. It did not address the needs of tenants, nor did it address what was perceived to be the most pressing problem at that time, that is, the rental shortage. The plan was inequitable. I am addressing the challenge of the hon. member in telling him what was wrong with the program. It has been demonstrated, and it has been the experience in countries such as the United States which have adopted the program, that it benefited those in the high tax brackets more than people who live in the area of the hon. member himself, an area which needs addressing at this time.
I think it can be stated fairly that over the years federal policies have helped to provide Canadians with a good and an adequate supply of housing at affordable prices. We have consistently followed directions which have provided housing for people who could not compete on the open market, and I have referred to them a number of times in my comments.
In conclusion I should like to indicate that in assuming responsibility for CMHC, I have had the opportunity of meeting with all of the provincial ministers of housing, with numerous local elected officials and local politicians from all parts of Canada. 1 am looking forward to their continued input and to hearing their opinions at the conference to which the hon. member for Vancouver East alluded, which will be held here in March. The conference will have an agenda which will be open to a wide spectrum of concerns of many Canadians, not just those identified by the hon. member in her remarks. We have asked that the organizers of the conference ensure adequate representation from the consumers and from people
Housing
from other sectors, such as producers and officials at the provincial and municipal levels. I am confident that that forum will provide a current review on the state of housing and the prospects for the 1980s which will be useful to the government in continuing its realistic and, I think, responsive role in co-operation with all others who are concerned about meeting the housing needs of Canadians.
I should like to comment now on another point raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North in respect of the Community Services Contribution Program. For the sake of the record I think I should indicate that the government is committed to the continuation of payments under that program until March, 1982, which commits the federal government to some $400 million toward the provision of services to municipalities and provinces which are their traditional responsibilities. That $400 million is a sum of money which normally and traditionally provinces and municipalities would have to provide themselves. This program will be continued until March of 1982. It is my expectation and hope that, with the co-operation and the input of, for example, the housing conference to which I have referred, the government will consider the provision of alternatives to shelter allowance. I am confident that the record of this government, in co-operation with CMHC, which has demonstrated its concern for addressing the housing needs of Canada in the financial and social areas, will continue to be a very good one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like briefly to deal with the motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), with respect to this government's incompetent housing policies. Last December, during the special debate on the economy, I stated that the government was totally estranged from all principles save one, the principle of power.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague says that the government has policies, albeit incompetent policies, which, he states in his motion:
-have led directly to soaring housing costs, plummeting housing starts, and critically low vacancy rates.
There can be no argument as to the existence of soaring housing costs, plummeting housing starts, and critically low vacancy rates. One has only to look to the Kerrisdale district in my riding to see what is happening to housing costs. One has only to look at the numbers that the minister has brought forward. By the way, I thought 1 heard him say that the target forecast by the Economic Council of Canada was for 180,000 housing starts which the minister thought was pretty good. On the other hand, the CMHC estimates for 1981 indicate there will be 264,000 houses needed. That is a shortfall, or a difference of opinion of some 84,000 units. There will be some very disappointed people this year.
The motion goes on to refer to critically low vacancy rates. I see that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) has left the House. 1 heard her telling us some very capitalistic

January 14, 1981
Housing
stories about herself and about the situation in Vancouver East, how she had purchased a house some time ago for S9.000 which is now worth something like $160,000. She also spoke about land banks. We have had that experience and it can be proven what a disaster land banks are and how they simply give governments the power to confer benefits upon their friends. We do not need land banks; we need people to buy land and to develop it and use it, not to bank it. That is what land in the housing market is for.
I should like to ask the member for Vancouver East, or any other Canadian, if they would be willing to sell their own house to foreigners. I heard the hon. member for Vancouver East mention that we should not allow foreigners to buy real estate in Canada. I wonder whether the member would sell her house to a foreigner. In the interests of providing cheaper housing, I wonder whether she would sell her house for less than market value. She told us about the beautiful capital gain she made. I wonder whether the hon. member for Vancouver East would like to pay tax on her capital gain or will take advantage of the proposals and avoid that tax.
I wonder if the hon. member for Vancouver East or any of her colleagues would consider themselves speculators because they happened to buy houses. After all, we would all be in that position if we own houses and happen to sell them for more; we would be guilty of being speculators. Yet the hon. member for Vancouver East and her colleagues all voted against a policy which the Conservative government put forth to provide relief through a mortgage interest and property tax credit scheme.
Vacancy rates have also been mentioned. I should like to refer to a rates list which was put out by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It indicates the vacancy rates on privately initiated units, including newly completed units available for rent, from 1978 to 1980. The next sheet shows a series of worse rates if newly completed buildings are excluded. When I say "worse", I mean lower vacancies. There are no less than seven metropolitan areas in Canada which in October,
1980, had vacancy rates of less than one per cent. The highest shown in any place is 5.8 per cent in Hull, although when that is combined with Ottawa it would be 4 per cent. Also there was Winnipeg and Windsor. Of course Windsor is a special case right now. In any event, only three places have over 5 per cent vacancy rates, and in all places, except those with vacancy rates below one per cent, the vacancy rates are falling.
We can trace the roots of the housing crisis back to 1971 when it really started in earnest after the government changed the generally accepted accounting principles and decreed that a loss on rental housing was not deductible from other income for tax purposes. But the government indicated that if one invested in a factory or a business and incurred a loss, then of course one could still deduct that from other income. How unfair to the taxpayers, how unfair to the tenants who were enjoying a goodly supply of rental housing in those days!
The clear and obvious result of this government action was a lack of investment in housing by high income Canadians.
Therefore, as a result of that there are now higher rents. In fact we got higher rents then. Because of higher rents and pressure on local and provincial governments in many areas of Canada we got rent controls.
However, the recent reintroduction of the MURB tax shelter was an attempt to correct this wrong and to attract once again the sector which was investing in housing into the housing market once again. It is not a sop to the rich, as my friend to the left tried to say. In saying that kind of thing, it would seem that my friends to the left do not want housing for their constituents. It is obvious. They have said again today that the government is not satisfying their needs. So, let us try the private sector and give them a little encouragement.
This action in 1971 was followed by various programs introduced by the government. There was AHOP which is interestingly enough known as "A FLOP" in some quarters. The hon. member for Simcoe North mentioned what a disaster AHOP was. But there will be 40,000 Canadian home owners in 1981 seeking to renew their AHOP mortgages. Most of them will probably walk away from their houses instead of renewing their mortgages. In 1982-83 there will be a further
46,000	Canadians wanting to renew their mortgages.
Then the government gave us ARP. It was a nice program which provided some housing. But interestingly enough, it absolutely required the continuation of high inflation rates in order to prevent the owners and builders of these developments from going bankrupt. Any policy which absolutely requires a continuing high rate of inflation is doomed. I suspect that ARP was doomed.
Then they gave us RRAP to help restore old housing in older areas of cities, because it was recognized that they were still good units. That resulted in huge rip-offs of elderly and unsuspecting home owners who wanted to have work done. Proper inspections were not conducted, and I have files in my office of problems created by RRAP.
The then minister of finance, Mr. Turner, gave us RHOSP which was supposed to encourage housing and stimulate the housing industry. All it really did was defer or discourage the purchase of a house at this point, because if one soon bought a house in Canada, one could not take advantage of the program. It was only if one deferred one's purchase for ten years that one could take advantage of RHOSP. We can look at what has happened to anyone who has taken advantage of this program. They may have received a few tax free dollars out of their RHOSPs, but they will not be able to buy much of a house with the funds now.
Then they gave us something called COOP. I guess it was co-op, really. It was a CMHC scheme for financing town houses in high cost areas, but one could not get into one of them unless one earned over $30,000 per year. Well, where is the aid for Canadian home owners in need? It is ridiculous.
Over the last decade CMHC made demands on the industry to continue to improve its requirements, so that finally costs were driven up. Now there are many cases where the 25 per cent income limit which used to be acceptable to CMHC
January 14, 1981

cannot be met. People now pay far more than a quarter of their income toward shelter costs. All these Liberal policies worked just as well as a spanner tossed into a machine works.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to a situation right here in Ottawa. Before I came here eight years ago, the Lebreton Flats area was cleared of what was then reasonably priced housing. It was held vacant by the government for ten years before any redevelopment was started on that site.
In the thirty-first Parliament the Progressive Conservative government proposed forward-looking policies such as mortgage interest and property tax credits. Their passage was shot down by members opposite and members to my left who do not care about providing housing for Canadians who need it. Those two groups defeated the budget proposals of the Clark government. Our budget was acknowledged by millions to be the first honest budget in over a decade, one which would have started Canada on the road to economic recovery.

Well then, what is to be done, Mr. Speaker?

What to do?

Eight years ago, in 1973, I stated in this House that I had a quick solution to the government's problem in the housing industry: "Get out of it!"

Get out of the industry. At that time the minister, Mr. Basford, took my advice in a perverted kind of way. He had the now Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation buy an industrial site in the city of Vancouver. It was 37 acres called Granville Island in the heart of his riding. He had the corporation move out the light industry which was there to make way for a park. Of course he hired the former president of the British Columbia Liberal party to be the director of that project. This island had nothing to do with housing or mortgages, but CMHC owns this island yet. The minister is looking embarrassed, I hope.
On this site they built stores which were rented in competition with other landlords renting stores. So we had merchants with subsidized rents, who were competing with merchants in other areas who were paying normal rents and paying the very taxes which were being used to subsidize these other merchants. We had a commercial area over there where people were paying full costs, customers were paying the full price, and over here we had subsidized rents. It is a ridiculous situation, especially for a supposed housing corporation.
This is a people place just waiting for a fire or other disaster to happen. There are stores, theatres and restaurants on this 37-acre island, which is at the end of a two-lane causeway. 1 shudder to think what will happen when we have a good fire going there. In Vancouver we call Granville Island "Basford's
Housing
boondoggle". Mr. Speaker, that is what that housing minister did to solve the question in Vancouver.
I think it is interesting that the present housing minister said in his remarks, "Vancouver, incidentally". Mr. Speaker, I hope that was a Freudian slip. But it is a typical display of the attitude of this government-"Vancouver, incidentally". Then he bragged to the House about having provided nearly 2,000 housing units. Well, there are individual companies and individual families who have provided, through the private sector, more than that number of units. I do not think it is anything to be proud of. On his own housing starts information it is truly a drop in the bucket.
At the same time as I was telling this former minister to get out of the housing industry, my former leader, the Hon. Robert Stanfield, was urging the government to wind up the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. Apparently they saw the error of their ways since, in fact, that ministry has now been eliminated. I do not know that all of its functions have disappeared, but that is what we can work toward.
Why is there a housing shortage in Canada, Mr. Speaker? Canadians certainly have the capacity to build an adequate supply of housing for Canadians. In fact we have an overcapacity under the present climate, and never have more Canadian entrepreneurs been building more homes for more Americans than ever before. What a situation! Now, because of even more government interference on another scale, we are watching the oil rigs following the entrepreneurs all the way to the border so that they can find oil for Americans, in greater numbers than ever before.
Affordable housing, Mr. Speaker, went up the flue with the value of the Canadian dollar. If I had more time, or if this was an economic debate, I could explain what happened with respect to housing and inflation, and interest rates and inflation. But perhaps others will contribute that to this debate.
We have the situation right now where rents are cheap in the industry. That is no accident, they are cheap because of rent controls. That was a two-edged favour that governments, in general, did for tenants. It made it easier for tenants. If you have an apartment you have got controlled rent, and it is fairly cheap. Even if your apartment is not under controls then you are probably competing with some that are. But the hooker is there are not any apartments available-less than 1 per cent in many places in Canada. So it is harder for the tenants because of these actions which governments have taken.
I say rents are cheap, Mr. Speaker. I can give as examples two apartments, one a rental apartment and one a condominium, let us say a nice two-bedroom condominium apartment in a city in Canada today priced at $100,000. If a person buys a condominium apartment for $100,000 with $20,000 down, his carrying costs will be over $1,300 a month, ignoring his $20,000 down payment. A similar apartment in comparable condition can be rented in any comparable city for half that amount because of these mixed up policies of various governments.

January 14, 1981
Housing
Ever since 1 came to Ottawa eight years ago people have been talking about the housing crisis. Of course it is a nice diversion for the government because it is nebulous. There is no housing problem in Canada today-there is a money problem. Mr. Speaker, if you have enough money you can buy anything or you can rent anything. You can go to Vancouver Quadra and I can show you a nice mansion you can buy for $1.2 million. I do not know if that will be in your budget. Or you can buy an adequate home for half a million dollars, or you can go into an older part of Kerrisdale and get a storey and a half older home for $280,000. The member for Vancouver East was telling us about her $160,000 house in what used to be the poorer area of town-the NDP section. They are buying 33-foot lots over there, Mr. Speaker, for over $100,000. In the western part of Vancouver Centre riding they are knocking down $240,000 houses so they can build two condominiums on those lots. Therefore, the land costs are $125,000 per unit.
1 looked up to see what I had said a few years ago. I just want to quote a couple of paragraphs from a speech 1 made here before. Not too many people quote me, and I like to do it once in a while. It was at a time when I was telling the government it should get out of the housing business. I said that the government could help us a lot by leaving us alone in our housing problems. This is what I said:
Disband the bureaucracies, cut taxes, and let us solve our own problems, with the interference of our local or provincial governments if we choose, but without federal interference, without federal bureaucrats taking our money from us in taxes and spending it as they want it spent rather than as we want it spent.
Later in the same speech I said this:
If it is really our desire to raise the material standard of living of poor people, rather than push them around and run their lives, then we should abandon the government policies that impoverish them. In place of the present mess of welfare schemes and housing schemes, we should give the poor people the cash presently spent on these things and let the poor people spend the cash in the ways that give them the greatest satisfaction. To build our preferred type of housing for the poor people and to hire thousands of bureaucrats to oversee them in these ghettos is wasteful.
My friends to the left would have the state take over the job more completely. I think that is a truism. As I said in my speech:
-the state is the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else;-
Later on I said:
-government. . . can destroy but not create, can build nothing of itself but can seize only what others have created;-
Finally, Mr. Speaker, this government could save itself a lot of problems and it could save Canadian home owners and tenants a great deal of grief if it would get out of the housing industry. Then the government could concentrate on real federal problems which government should be considering, like inflation, unemployment, and defence.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) for giving a member from Quebec
the opportunity to say just how pleased we are with the housing policy of this government, not that it cannot be improved, of course, but I do feel that, at the present time, as a Liberal member from Quebec, I welcome the housing policy of our government and would like to repeat the remarks I made during the debate on Bill C-20 to the effect that, according to the figures put out by the well-known organization called the OECD, Canada ranks first in terms of the ratio of people per room. Their standards are recognized internationally; Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg and other countries are covered in that study. We must recognize as well that Canada ranked first, again according to the figure of the OECD for 1980, in terms of housing units made available to Canadians.
As far as available housing is concerned, I suspect my hon. colleague is mistaken in his interpretation of Canadian problems. There may be housing problems in some cities, some areas, but those problems are in the process of being solved thanks to the wise policy of the minister; still I feel that the problems are merely local. If we look at Canada as a whole, that is, if we look at it from the point of view of federal MPs, we realize that Canadians in fact have a very high standard of housing.
For my part, 1 can only rejoice in the fact that in the riding of Mercier several new starts have been made in the last few months, and that, in the Montreal area, generally speaking, the densification program, that is, the construction of 10,000 units, is now in progress; the city of Montreal, as well as the federal authorities, of course, say they are very pleased with the program that is now under way in a metropolitan area that is comparable to Vancouver and Toronto. In that respect, we certainly have no reason to complain, as representatives of the Montreal area, about the policy of the minister responsible for housing.
In any event, I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to invite those of my colleagues who may be experiencing temporary difficulties in their areas, to spend some time in Montreal since we can offer them the advantage of housing that is comfortable, of excellent quality and at reasonable prices. It might perhaps foster mutual understanding amongst Canadians. I invite them to come and visit the province of Quebec. Our housing supply is quite adequate, and they could perhaps enjoy temporarily another way of life, of leisure, until such time as the situation improves in their own areas.
As members of Parliament, we must recognize that there are problems, that some developing cities actually suffer from shortages. But it must be stressed that the problem is localized and that remedial action is being taken.
In Quebec, we have had a few problems, it cannot be denied. My colleagues are no doubt aware of the farm zoning act; in any event, the only Quebec opposition member has certainly
January 14, 1981

heard about it and will no doubt have to speak to it in a coming election campaign. That act gave rise to certain problems with respect to housing, that is, land speculation, and has slowed down development in the outlying areas of Montreal. However, I must add that in Quebec we have not experienced the same serious and extensive land speculation problems as other provinces. I think my colleagues would be dishonest if they were to blame the federal government for such speculation. They should ask the provincial rather than the federal authorities to control such speculation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) or the hon. member for Simcoe North would be well advised, 1 think, Mr. Speaker, to discuss with provincial representatives the increased costs and the shameless land speculation. The greater part of the cost of these houses or housing units consists of land costs. How can a country as vast as Canada suffer from a lack of land, Mr. Speaker? The only answer is speculation.
It is understandable that Switzerland, because of its size, should experience such a situation, but as representatives of the federal government, we find it astonishing that Canada, the second largest country in the world, should be short of land. And I do not think that the answer to the speculation problem is a housing policy. Our friends opposite, the Progressive Conservatives who are also quite chummy with the private sector might be well advised perhaps to have some private talks with their colleagues especially on the matter of those reasonable profits about which my honourable colleague from Vancouver East could tell them a lot because if her property went up from $9,000 to $150,000, I am wondering if in all honesty any true New Democrat could sell his house at such an exorbitant price and make such unreasonable profits. Therefore I wonder why in those provinces with a New Democratic representation no action is taken to put an end to such activities on the part of speculators, on the part of a sector of private enterprise that sometimes takes advantage of the consumers. 1 do not think, Mr. Speaker, that public funds contributed to by all taxpayers across Canada should be used to quench the greed of these speculators.
On the other end, Mr. Speaker, coming back to the subject of housing and the allegations contained in the resolution of my colleague from Simcoe I must say that at the present time, the policy of this government just as before, is geared to helping people become owners of a reasonably-priced good quality home.
However, I do not believe that a reasonable policy should promote access to housing at any price, at the expense of other taxpayers and underprivileged Canadians. Mr. Speaker, we must recognize the fact that some people are less privileged than others as far as housing is concerned. As I pointed out in this House in November, 1979, there are really three groups in our society with special housing problems. These include, first of all, the Indians or the native people of Canada who have
Housing
benefited from special programs. I should add that, in my opinion, the minister is well aware of this situation and in co-operation with his colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), he developed specific programs and policies on behalf of these people as soon as the Liberal party regained power. There are two more groups which are just as badly off in my opinion, namely, low-income women with dependants and senior citizens, who both have housing problems. I believe that this government is aware of their plight.
I know that considerable efforts have been made by most Canadians to help these groups. More work will have to be done, but I believe that this can come about only with the co-operation of the provincial governments. These are social measures. Therefore, if we want to stay within the spirit of federalism, I think all action in this area should be taken with the co-operation of the provinces.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to report that the Mercier constituency has had a very successful experience with co-operative housing. This has allowed and will continue to allow low wage earners to purchase property at reasonable prices and to become home owners, in multiple housing projects, it must be admitted, but they can still live in their own homes even though they do not have the high incomes mentioned by my colleague.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to come back now to the question of housing needs in Canada. Should we go on building to meet the needs of industry or of the people? As hon. members are certainly aware, there has been a decrease in the birth rate, our population is getting smaller and our way of life has changed. In this regard, we have on the one hand greater mobility and on the other hand, smaller families than ten or 20 years ago, and as a result of a declining birth rate, an aging population.
Therefore I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a wise housing policy should reflect these demographic phenomena and meet a new demand, and I think that the minister is very conscious of these facts. There is no doubt in my mind that as a former mayor he will be able to meet the demand by promoting the necessary programs. On the other hand, I am somewhat surprised that my colleague from Simcoe North should mention a sudden shortage and call this debate on housing policy, even though 1 welcome this opportunity to provide information to the Canadian public. 1 would like to point out to the hon. member that, in 1978, we had just about the same shortages, the same increase, and that over the last ten years, nine of the 20 surveys which the Canada Housing and Mortgage Corporation conducts twice a year, or about 50 per cent of them, have shown the same results. The situation is therefore not unusual. It is certainly not alarming, and 1 would like people to know that, although we are now debating this issue quite calmly and with great interest, there is no reason to sound the alarm for the future because, considering the problems now facing the

January 14, 1981
Housing
world economy, we cannot truthfully say the problem of housing in Canada is crucial. In fact, for the sake of my colleague from Vancouver East I would like to mention that we have received encouraging figures showing that there has been a recovery in areas formerly plagued with real shortages. This means that in cities such as Vancouver, between January and December the building activity increased 40 per cent. In Victoria the increase was 200 per cent. And somewhere else where the demand is greater it was up 133 per cent. According to my colleague from Simcoe North, a greater demand is supposed to put pressure on prices, push up prices of housing units and put them out of reach of the people. It would seem that Canadians can afford to buy those houses, since in areas where few housing units are available a high level of building activity is recorded. Just the same, for the benefit of my colleague from Toronto, I would like to point out a few facts from an organization which he knows quite well, 1 think, since there are two members from Toronto. 1 refer to the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada. I am repeating myself somewhat, Mr. Speaker, since those facts confirm our apprehensions.
Demographics, family formation ... is predicted by all forecasters to bring about a widespread reduction in total demand for housing by the middle of the next decade-
And later:
-it's inevitable that by the mid-1980's, demand for housing will be less over all. In short, the peak has passed.

We are not the only ones to be aware of the situation which is due to a falling birth-rate, to a decrease in family sizes, new marriages and new people coming into the market to purchase new houses and 1 think that the department, in its wisdom, meets the demand. I did not hear my colleague suggest solutions which without increasing the deficit would not cost anything to the taxpayers. The only imaginative solution found by our colleagues, which will surely bring back to them some bitter memories, was the 18-cent tax on gas which I think was not very well received by the Canadian people. The $2 billion or $3 billion intended for the friends of the Progressive Conservative Party went up in smoke in December, 1979, and I think that their housing program did not meet the needs of Canadians who, of course, proved this assumption to be right.
Mr. Speaker, coming back to my colleague from Vancouver East who pointed out a while ago how many underprivileged groups should be provided with adequate housing and so on, 1 think that the government in its wisdom each year earmarks some funds, and the minister was quite explicit about it a while ago, to increase the number of low-cost housing units. The burden should, just the same, be acceptable to Canadians. We would like to provide all Canadians with first-rate housing but we will not be really in a position to do so before a few years.
In the meantime, I ask her to consider the cost of her proposals.
It seems that NDP members have a lot of imagination when it comes to new policies, but they have much less when they have to put a price tag on these policies. Therefore, ! suggest to them to consider, as an alternative, the solutions offered by our Creditiste colleagues who had a rather peculiar approach concerning the acquisition of funds. I do not see any other alternative, because for the time being 1 think our economy can in most cases meet the needs of Canadians but cannot surely provide a higher standard of living than any other country of the world. I think that our colleagues are just popularity seeking when they refer to some aid to Third World countries where people have nothing to eat and no roof over their heads. And I think that a responsible government should not incense Third World countries by spending moneys that might be deemed unreasonable in relation to the whole budget.
In my view, the Minister of Finance has proposed, with the support of the minister in charge of housing, very sound housing measures in his budget. And were I to believe that some people even outside my constituency-because I feel 1 can speak for the Canadian people-were experiencing a particular problem, I would be the first to rise and ask that such deficiencies be corrected. I do not think we have had that kind of shortage over these last ten years. Housing costs have increased less than the inflation rate, the existing housing supplies and the shortage are almost the same as they were ten years ago. In other words the shortage fluctuated. We have always responded to these shortages, which means that they will be made up.
In conclusion, I hope that land will become available in provinces other than Quebec at more reasonable prices. I feel that we should urge our colleagues from those provinces to look into these matters along with their provincial counterparts. I for one am ready to discuss this with them.
I thank the minister for his excellent policies and for the opportunity he has given me to exchange views with my colleagues on an issue of national significance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join in the debate today and to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis). We are debating an opposition motion which reads as follows:
That this House condemns the government for its incompetent housing policies, which have led directly to soaring housing costs, plummeting housing starts, and critically low vacancy rates.
Before I get into the meat of my remarks, I should like to touch upon a couple of items raised first of all by the minister and secondly by the hon. member for Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette). I know that the hon. member for Mercier will be pleased to learn that there is at least one constituent from Mercier watching her this afternoon. The housing starts in the riding of Mercier that she and this government were taking credit for were in fact instigated by TUnion Nationale govern-
January 14, 1981

ment in the province of Quebec which subsidized the first $7,000 of the mortgages. One of the hon. member's constituents called in about this very quickly in order to set the record straight.
1 should like to thank the minister responsible for CMHC for the history lesson, much of which was contained in the organization's annual report of 1979. I know that David Mansur, the first president of CMHC, will be extremely proud of the minister and that history lesson that he gave.
I know that the housing critic for this party will echo my remarks when I say that we are pleased that a conference has been set for March. The agenda is wide-ranging and the conference is well planned. We on this side of the House hope it is successful and that the people of Canada can look forward to some very real results. I cannot support the view of the member of the NDP who suggested that the conference should be called immediately. This conference has been arranged and is ready to go, and I wish it all the best.
The right to own decent affordable housing has been a generally accepted principle in this country for a long time. That is until now. No one can argue that shelter is an absolute necessity. However, we are now faced with a housing problem. It could be far worse than the problems faced after World War II when CMHC was established in 1945. We are faced with policies of a government which cannot tell us that it really supports the fundamental right or freedom of every Canadian to acquire a home, to own property, a right which most Canadians have taken for granted.
At this time in our history when we are all concerned with the changes being recommended by the Liberal government, fundamental changes to our nation, the right to private ownership of property is being eroded by a government that will not give us the guarantee of private ownership in writing, but whose floating bank rate policy has skyrocketed interest rates to unprecedented heights making the purchase of a simple home virtually impossible for most young Canadians.
It was once considered government policy to encourage and stimulate housing production. I believe that was the initial mandate given to CMHC. It was once policy that CMHC should concern itself with social housing needs. To some extent, I admit that progress has been made. Over the Christmas break I spent a delightful morning at one of the senior citizens' residents put up by the Ontario Housing Corporation and financed by CMHC. Those people are well housed and enjoy their residence. I had a high regard for the role which CMHC has played in the housing field, until recently. However, in its role as an agency of federal social policy on shelter, it has failed miserably. Whether this failure is due to the added burden placed on it or whether the government just cannot decide whether the corporation should be a financial institution, a social agency or a real estate brokerage firm, I am not sure. The minister responsible for housing has repeatedly said that it is not a function of government to build houses or apartment buildings. Is it the function of the government to depress the construction and real estate industries?
Housing
CMHC is quickly becoming very large in the real estate business. As of June, 1980, by the minister's figures, CMHC had on hand more than 36,000 housing units across the country. Roughly 16,000 units were acquired just last year. If the June figures are any indication, I am sure it has probably picked up another 10,000 units by now. It makes CMHC a very large property owner, property it just cannot afford to carry or own. CMHC lost about a half a billion dollars in 1979. We do not know yet what it lost in 1980. But the lack of national housing plans just allows this condition to worsen.
Just for a moment, let us go back to the problem of affordability. Owning a home was once the dream of most Canadians. 1 believe it still is. Public opinion polls show that 90 per cent of young Canadians want to own their own homes, but that dream is becoming a nightmare.
For example, can a family with an average income of $22,000-obviously one with both husband and wife working-afford to buy a home at an average cost in metropolitan Toronto of $98,000-with which the minister is familiar- carrying a first-mortgage interest rate of at least 15.25 per cent? That was the lowest rate I could find today, and that is just gambling on a one-year term.
The hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in his role of housing critic just a short time ago felt that 14 per cent interest rates were high and that 30 per cent of income allotted for shelter cost was too high. How does the minister feel about 15.5 per cent and 16 per cent interest rates, and roughly 40 per cent to 50 per cent of income being spent on the most basic housing? Where is the minister now? Why is he not speaking out in favour of the young people who cannot afford a home?
There is another fellow who sits over there in the front row. I am speaking of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). He was the finance critic when he sat in opposition. I sat with him on the Commons finance committee. I was there on October 30 when he made his profound statement. At the time he was talking about a 14 per cent prime interest rate. He said:
-it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs, increases in the cost of living, it will bring the housing industry to a halt, it will put housing beyond the reach of most middle and lower-income Canadians, it will hurt small business and it will hurt farmers, and add to the cost of food.
Where is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce now?

speechtext: He was going to resign.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
That is right. We watched that infamous program where he said "if interest rates go up, I will resign". He is still sitting there, and I hope the people in Windsor remember that.
An NHA mortgage in 1975 averaged 10.4 per cent. If that mortgage were renegotiated today, the home owner would be looking at roughly increased mortgage payments of approximately 25 per cent. The financial shock which these increases cause on the family turns their dreams into hideous nightmares. For example, a $50,000 mortgage at 10.4 per cent

January 14, 1981
Housing
amortized over 20 years costs $483.77 per month in interest and principal. Today at 15.25 per cent, that same mortgage with the same term costs $650.54. That is a $167 increase, and this government says, "They are earning more money now. They can afford to pay". Except the government does not figure on people having families, and that is an added cost. The cost of fuel has risen along with all other costs. It just does not add up. It costs almost $200 more a month for the same mortgage.
We all know about AHOP. I have discussed this topic many times in the House, as has my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe North who was the official opposition's critic for housing, and a number of other members in the House. It is not "a-hope". It is AHOP. The minister hopes it will disappear; I know that, but it will not. You have got it, and you will have to face it. The minister has come up with a little scheme of helping cases of hardship. Up to December, in the Toronto area, only 55 applications had been made. Each individual has to bow down to the local CMHC manager and say, "Please, sir, may 1 have a little grant from you?" That is very demeaning. The minister has been very careful in saying that he will handle each case on an individual basis. That is just like giving band-aids. He is not looking at the problem at all. He is not really caring about those people who are having one very tough time. We hear words such as, "Come and see me, and I will give you a little money. I will see what I have here and I will see if I can help you out on an individual basis." I have been hammering away at this with the minister for a very long time. The inaction has been very obvious.
The AHOP program looked extremely good on paper when it was brought in. But something this government continues to do with programs it brings in is to forget the human element. A program looks great on paper. It appears super when the scribes up over the Speaker's throne write about it. The press release looks fantastic. However, the government forgets the human element. It does not look at people. It takes them out of everything.
Earlier the minister said that they are looking at the problem, or that they are monitoring the situation. CMHC is now selling vacant units in the region of Peel, which I partially represent, for $5,000 to $8,000 less than the original home owners paid for them a few years ago. This is a vibrant real estate market in a metropolitan area. It is a suburban area where costs have gone up for those units, yet they are being sold at $8,000 less than was originally paid for them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: Who is paying the difference?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
We know who is paying the difference. That is why they are walking away. The minister knows that. He cannot fool the people any more. There are all kinds of vacancies there. It is easier to walk away than renegotiate a loan or go on your knees to CMHC asking for a little more to help you out. Walking away is easier and much cheaper than foreclosure.
I hope the minister will come out of the housing conference with a true national housing policy, one the urban centres can latch on to. One problem is that metropolitan housing authorities cannot count on the government. They do not know if next year they will get any money. Social housing has been provided through their housing departments, but they do not know whether they will get any aid. It is at the whim of the minister. We have seen evidence of this time and time again.
Low and moderate income housing is desperately needed in this country. It has been provided in metropolitan areas up until now, but they cannot plan any longer. There is no housing planning, no program whereby they can say, "This is what we are going to do one, two, three years down the road." Until something like that is in place, we will continue with the housing mess than we now find in Canada. I urge the minister to come out of that conference with a national housing plan which makes sense.
New housing starts are down. I do not have to repeat the figure. The minister knows that in 1980 they were down to
160,000	from almost 200,000 in 1979. The estimated requirement was 260,000. There has been a tremendous shortfall. With housing starts running lower than required, the cost of housing is increasing. Property taxes are increasing. Double digit inflation and energy costs are affecting family incomes. It is time for the government to take a long hard look at how it can help these home owners.
I listened earlier to criticism of the mortgage interest and property tax credit program. I heard it said that that would not help the renters. Renters are already being helped. The landlord who owns a building can write off the interest on his mortgage now as a business expense. He can write off the property tax as a business expense. Therefore, renters are now getting that benefit, and have been getting it for a number of years. They receive a reduced rent in that way. We say let's help the young people get into housing now.
The minister says this is a program for the wealthy. That is utter nonsense. Wealthy people do not have mortgages on their homes. They have paid them off. Believe me, it is the desire of every person to pay off his mortgage. If a wealthy person does have a home mortgage, you can bet your boots his money has gone into investments and the interest can be written off as a business expense. Therefore, the rich are now being helped, so don't hand the Canadian public that baloney. They will not buy it.
I want the minister to come to the riding of Brampton-Georgetown and tell that to the young people who want to buy homes. The program introduced by the Progressive Conservatives which the NDP and the Liberals defeated, shot right down, would have reduced interest rates by 3 per cent. That would have allowed another group of young people to qualify for mortgages.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: Order, please. 1 regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate this afternoon. Maybe because I
January 14, 1981

have a reputation of not always saying good things about the government, there will be some credibility to the remarks I am going to make. 1 personally am very proud, and 1 say this very sincerely, of the efforts of this and previous governments in the past 12 years in the housing field in this country.
I, as a builder and contractor, could sing the blues about the state of the construction industry today. But that does not get away from the fact that housing starts last year, 1980, and let's put this into perspective, dropped 18 per cent. The figures for December have just been released. There was an 18 per cent drop in a year when everybody acknowledges interest rates were high. Therefore, there was a deterrent to people finding mortgages for new housing. However, using the figure quoted by the previous speaker of 160,000 starts, if we compare that to our neighbour, the United States, I say thank God we are in Canada and thank God we have the policies we do in this country. Frankly, one of the reasons there may have been some reduction in housing construction in the last little while is because there was such a surge in housing construction in previous years.
There has been reference to AHOP, a program which I say very seriously I support 100 per cent. I support that program because it has provided housing for a very large number of persons who would not have been able to afford it without the support of that program. If, as a result, there has been a relatively small percentage of persons who have not been able to continue in their housing accommodation, and let's be blunt, at least for the period of time they lived in those houses they had housing they could afford. It was good housing. If they have had to walk away because their salaries have not increased as anticipated, it is one of the facts of life that we do not always get everything we want. At least we have assisted 19 persons for every one person who has had to walk away from his housing.
I want to come back in a minute to the cost of AHOP but, talking about availability of housing, I wish to put a few things on the record. I wonder if the opposition realizes that five miles from here one can buy a new three-bedroom house for $22,000. I am putting these figures on the record intentionally. Some will say, "But who wants to live five miles from here?" I am telling hon. members that some 30 years ago when I built my house, I had to build it some 25 miles outside Montreal because that was the only place I could find a piece of ground which was cheap enough in those days. I suggest that one of the problems today when people are looking at housing costs is that everyone expects to live in downtown Ottawa. Under those circumstances I say they should be prepared to pay the price. However, houses are there at reasonable prices if people want them.
While talking about new houses let me mention, for example, that on the south shore of Montreal one can buy a brand new pre-fab three bedroom house, equipped with a refrigerator and stove, for $34,000, with a 5 per cent down payment. What more could anyone want today? If one cannot buy the same
Housing
house in Edmonton, then I say, "Too bad". I know what is going on there. We know why prices are high, but another reason prices are so high in Alberta is that there has been a surge in building which has created a shortage of building tradesmen. As a result we have to bring into this country various construction tradesmen to work in the province of Alberta. One of the problems we have is that our construction worker is not necessarily mobile. Do I not know it? 1 live just outside Montreal, and I have waited precisely nine months for an electrician to do work in my house. I suggest that all is not that bad in the construction industry when one has to wait that period of time to get construction help.
I also want to mention that for those who perhaps cannot afford $22,000 or $34,000 for new housing, not very many miles from where I am standing right now, one can also buy partly finished houses. The exteriors are complete, but there is interior finishing to do. The cost of these houses is $14,000 to $18,000. I remember also some 30 years ago that when we wanted to build houses most of us had to take shells and finish the interiors ourselves. Some probably even had to build kitchen cupboards themselves. I suggest that people today are not prepared to build their own kitchen cupboards. In fact most expect everything to be finished, including the painting, the tiling, and even the carpeting on the floor. It is a question of what we want. Part of the reason prices have increased substantially is that people have demanded more in their housing.
1 wanted to discuss the cost of AHOP a little bit, but before I get into that I wish to talk about mortgage insurance. Mortgage loan insurance was introduced in 1954 when the National Housing Act was amended to allow the chartered banks to enter the residential mortgage lending field. The banks had previously been excluded from direct mortgage lending under the terms of the Bank Act. By protecting the lender against the risk of loss, NHA mortgage insurance encourages approved lenders to invest in mortgages. Mortgage insurance fees paid by borrowers to CMHC are accumulated in a mortgage insurance reserve fund.
I want to talk about that fund in a minute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext: A bankrupt fund.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED INCOMPETENT HOUSING POLICIES
speechtext:
I will repeat the comment of the hon. member opposite. He said, "A bankrupt fund". I want to refer specifically to that point. Lenders may claim against the fund in the event a borrower defaults on his payments and foreclosure results. The mortgage insurance fee is usually 1 per cent of the amount of the loan, and is included in the loan amount. Various ministers responsible for CMHC over the years will be able to substantiate that, over the years, I have suggested that the 1 per cent fee was too high and that it should be reduced to one-half of 1 per cent. The reason I did that was that there was relatively no risk, and a huge fund exceeding $600 million accumulated from the insurance premiums which were being paid on mortgages.
As late as the fall of last year, in writing to the minister responsible for CMHC, who spoke earlier this afternoon, I

January 14, 1981
Housing
said that I would vigorously oppose the imposition of any additional charge for regular mortgage insurance fees which should not be regarded as a source of funds to ease a liquidity problem caused by government policy.
The point is-and 1 go back now to AHOP-AHOP was a social program which was brought in, and the insurance fee was 1 per cent as in the case of regular housing. There has been acknowledged a far greater percentage of walk-aways under AHOP than in relation to regular mortgages. I have stated-and I mean this very sincerely-that this is a social cost, and it must be recognized as such. As a result I have opposed the increase of the insurance fee even on AHOP housing because I believe that, if it is a social program, then the 90 per cent or 95 per cent of those who successfully have used AHOP should not be paying an additional fee to cover those who, unfortunately, do not receive the increases in income which enable them to retain their houses.
The extent of the AHOP problem was certainly aggravated by economic difficulties, regional situations, and at least to some extent by related government policies. We know that this has certainly been the case in southern Ontario, and it certainly has been in Quebec where the provincial political situation has exerted an appreciable influence on the success of the program.
1 would like to read an extract from a letter which the minister was kind enough to send me about two months ago, regarding the mortgage insurance fees charged by CMHC. The extract reads as follows:
it would be inequitable for CMHC to raise its mortgage insurance premiums to recover the losses incurred in insuring loans under the Assisted Home Ownership Program and the Assisted Rental Program. As you point out in your letter, these were social programs and accordingly, their social cost should not be borne by those seeking National Housing Act mortgage insurance, but by the government. Unfortunately, as you know, no provision was made for this at the time these programs were introduced, with the result that the Mortgage Insurance Fund has already borne this risk and is now bearing the cost.
As far as normal insured loans are concerned, it is my view that the insurance premiums charged should reflect risk and the M1F should be operated on a self-financing risk-pooling basis. I do not believe that there is justification for taxpayers at large to subsidize the cost of mortgage insurance. It was in this context that the current study on the NHA insurance fee structure was initiated.
The gentleman across the way spoke about the huge losses to CMHC resulting from the acquisitions of these properties, but even-and the hon. member should read the newspapers occasionally-the newspaper columnists, who sometimes have a tendency to exaggerate, have talked about the cost last year as being in the order of $100 million. The figure may or may not be correct. 1 will not be the one to say that $100 million is not a very large sum of money, but 1 will put it in context. Fortunately as a result of policy-and it was not originally intended to be that way-we had a fund of some $600 million which was able to be used for the very purpose of helping a good social program to acquire these properties and at the present time to return these properties in an orderly fashion to the market.
While I am on the subject-and I cannot resist poking a finger at the opposition for its inconsistency-they may recall about two years ago when Canada Mortgage and Housing
Corporation was attempting to dispose of some of its portfolio on housing that there was one very large housing project in Montreal which was put up for tender. It made good sense to any one who looked at the figures that CMHC should sell that property at a loss. What was the reaction of the Tory party at that time? The spokesman for the Tory party stood up in this House and objected strongly to the fact that CMHC was trying to reduce its portfolio. The reason was simply that the spokesman for the official opposition was afraid that the rents of the persons occupying those apartments would increase when that building belonged in the private sector instead of being in the portfolio of CMHC.
1 call that plain hypocrisy. As a result the taxpayer-after all, this is CMHC absorbing this loss, and CMHC belongs to the taxpayer-had to absorb unnecessary costs because of the resistance put up at that time to the disposal of the portfolio when prices were reasonably good. 1 suggest that if CMHC had not met resistance in those days to selling off some of its housing, it would have been in an even better position than it is in today because, after all, its problem today is not loss, its problem is liquidity, and there must be a very clear distinction between these two figures. For the opposition to talk about a half billion dollar loss is absolutely garbage, and I have no other term for it.
I do want to put on the record, when talking about mortgage interest, a few statistics which might be of interest, and I address these remarks particularly to members of the NDP so they can think about what direction precisely they want to suggest the government take. I wish to read one paragraph from a letter to me from CMHC. These are figures provided by CMHC in January of 1981. It reads:
The total cost of a I per cent, one year subsidy for all new mortgages in 1981 for new housing with loans of up to $50,000 per unit is estimated to be $75 million. The total cost of a 1 per cent subsidy to home owners for first time renewal of mortgages on housing in 1981 is estimated at $100 million. If a 1 per cent subsidy were provided to all home owners renewing in 1981, the total cost is estimated to be $125 million.
Armed with those figures we should make up our minds on whether we feel that that is a direction in which we want to move. I realize the hardships experienced at present because of mortgage rates running at 15 per cent, but also today it is possible to get a one-year mortgage. In fact the one or two year mortgages are at lower rates than the five-year mortgages, and 1 feel it is not particularly risky to be taking a one-year mortgage at this time, even at the higher rate, in anticipation of reduced interest rates one year from now.
When I built my house I did not have any choice because 1 could not get a one-year mortgage. I had to get a five year mortgage. So 1 was stuck for five years, whether I liked it or not. A person taking a mortgage today has the option of taking a one-year or two-year mortgage. I found it most interesting that the interest rate on a one-year or two-year mortgage is half of 1 per cent or even 1 per cent less than the interest rate on a five-year mortgage.
January 14, 1981

1 want to discuss some of the efforts made by CMHC in trying to help the construction industry, and I will refer specifically to renovation work because, after all, as a builder, if 1 cannot get orders for new housing, I have to find something to do, and one of the things I can do is to look around for alternative construction work, and surely renovation is one of the things I can do.
The main support of the federal government to residential renovation is through the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, or RRAP. Here I want to insert a remark concerning what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell). There has been no reduction whatsoever in the allocation of funds for RRAP. It is completely untrue to make that suggestion. As a result, I suggest that a little more publicity would not do any more harm.
I will read from a letter from the minister responsible for CMHC as follows:
Under that program, CMHC may lend home owners in designated areas up to $10,000 for improvements. Of this amount, a maximum of $3,750 may be forgiven. For rental properties, landlords may obtain loans from private lenders for rehabilitation work, and are eligible for CMHC forgivable loans for up to 50 per cent of the cost of repairs to a maximum of $2,500 per unit. In the current year, some $250 million has been allocated for RRAP.
Then the construction industry must make sure that those funds are used. Home improvement loans made by bankers or approved instalment credit agencies may be guaranteed by the home improvement loan insurance fund established for that purpose by CMHC. The maximum loan amount is $10,000 and the insurance fee is 1 per cent of the principal borrowed, in other words, the same percentage fee as applies on regular mortgages.
There are many other areas in which CMHC has provided invaluable assistance, not only to the construction industry but to the home owner. 1 want to speak for a moment about a favourite program-

-the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, or RRAP. This assistance is intended for individuals, either owner-occupiers or lessors, rather than for large organizations or other levels of government. That is why the program does not lend itself to public advertising in the same way as the inauguration of a new apartment complex financed by the federal government.
The program is intended to provide financial assistance for home improvements to individuals or families of average income in designated rural areas. Assistance is provided in the form of loans of up to $10,000, of which a maximum of $3,500 may be forgiven, according to the applicant's income. In the province of Quebec, the program is administered by municipalities which are compensated for the administration costs incurred. This program has been a big success particularly in my riding where farmers have made good use of it. I commend the minister for it.
Housing

I should also like to make reference to CHIP because, after all, that program is also a construction program and it has been extremely successful. I received from the minister a month ago the notification that some three-quarters of a million cheques have been issued under this program. The assistance amounts to over a quarter of a billion dollars. I suggest once again that, for those of us who were in the construction industry, these are the means by which we try to get over the immediate problem of the drop in new housing construction. Since I am back to speaking about new housing construction, 1 should like to put on the record some rather interesting points concerning the number of houses that have been built in 1980.
