speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I commence my remarks I should like to say that I am usually happy to hear from the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). I know he was heavily involved in the construction industry. He has been out of the construction industry for some time and presumably he has been away from his own constituency for a long time, and that is too bad.
If he had talked to some of the young people who were conned into buying AHOP properties by the advertising put out by the corporation which gave them a hope and a dream that housing would go up in value and that their investment in real estate would rise in value, that it would give them a place to stand and it would give them security so that they could hold their heads high in the community, if he talked to them repossessions than I would dare to count, I wonder if the to leave them because they could not finance them because the corporation had polluted the marketplace so that the homes they bought could not be sold because there were so many new homes around because builders had received guarantee insurance on mortgages from CMHC to the extent that in some areas, particularly in the region of Peel, there are more repossessions than I would dare to count, I wonder if the would continue saying this was a great program. I wonder if he would say that it was great for these people to have homes for a short while. It is too bad we let them have their homes and their dreams for a short while and we allowed those dreams to be crushed.
The hon. member says that AHOP is a social policy. Is it the social policy of CMHC to con people into putting $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 investment down on a property and to have that investment washed away by marketing schemes allowing builders to over build in an area and thus to destroy the real estate market in that area? Is that social policy? Is that Liberal social policy? That is exactly the problem.
On Saturday a man by the name of Mr. Defrates came into my office. He purchased a condominium unit in the Streets-

January 14, 1981
Housing
ville area of Mississauga. It was a single family house condominium. There are 35 units in that condominium which were originally financed by National Trust. He paid $77,900 for his unit. He put $10,000 down and financed $67,900 on paper at 9.5 per cent. There was so much overbuilding in the area that the project- and 1 have seen it; it is a lovely project-just did not sell. As a matter of fact, of the 35 units developed, only seven were sold. Somewhere along the line the mortgage company rented another five units but the rest remained vacant, and the keys were turned over to CMHC in May, 1980.
CMHC took possession and completed the units. They were painted and decorated, the grass was cut, and they were left vacant. The units have since been appraised at $55,000, not the original $77,900. But even at that price the corporation will not put them on the market. The corporation will not even rent them. The corporation has left those houses vacant. They are being heated over this cold winter. The corporation shovels the snow over this cold winter. It uses the money of the people of Canada over this cold winter. The corporation has no program for the proper disposal of these properties on the real estate market it destroyed by handing out mortgage insurance for various developments which took place.
We can say that people make mistakes, that businesses make mistakes, and that corporations make mistakes. Surely CMHC can be excused for its mistakes, but in March, 1977, in the region of Peel, James Crozier, the director of social services, filed with CMHC a complete dossier and brief on the AHOP problem, the condominium problem and development problems which the corporation created in that region. One would have thought that with a local social service agency setting out clearly the problems which were occurring at that time, that CMHC would have ceased giving undertakings to insure. But, no, the game was ongoing. There was AHOP and the graduated payment plan mortgage scheme; various great schemes developed. We all know how many capital letters these fellows opposite combined in the management of this corporation. I have mentioned AHOP and GMPP or whatever it is, but there is NIP, RRAP, and others. All of these schemes were put together to do something, but certainly in the region of Peel they were criticized. The problem was pointed out in March, 1977, yet the corporation went ahead and continued to finance more and more building, and more and more families wound up getting sucked in and repossessions took place.
1 live in the southern part of Mississauga on the lake. Just outside the old town of Port Credit there is a development
called Balsam Woods which was started back in 1974. It is a townhouse condominium complex. They never could sell Balsam Woods. They sold the homes, nice modest condominium homes, but people walked away from them. So, they sold them again. Last year 1 was involved with my church in placing a Vietnamese family coming to Canada. CMHC gave me the opportunity to rent one of those units for that family. The manager of CMHC gave me the keys of four units. He said, "Don, take your pick". I visited the complex and I walked among beautiful homes which were lying vacant. Some of them have been rented, some of them have been sold, but the project never got off the ground. The project had insurance undertakings in 1974 and 1975, but it did not get off the ground. Yet, in 1977 and 1978 the corporation continued to give insurance undertakings. The problem is compounded by the high interest rate policy of the government.
Yesterday in the House the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) confirmed that high interest rate policy when he confirmed his policy of directing the Bank of Canada to use its treasury marketing system to keep the rate of interest high. So, the interest rates are 15 or 15.5 per cent, and there is no government policy to reduce them for home owners. They thought that our suggestion in the last Parliament of an interest tax credit would help the rich. It was designed-and everyone involved in housing knows it-to help young couples pay the interest costs. With interest rates at 15 per cent today, it would have meant 3.5 per cent off the cost of carrying a home. That was a help, but is there anything similar from this government?
The budget of CMHC is in excess of $1.1 billion. Certainly it would carry a great deal of the cost of helping young people with the interest on their mortgages. In many parts of Canada they do not need the Government of Canada in the housing business any longer. For example, the government of British Columbia has surpluses. It can finance housing in Vancouver. I know there is a problem in Vancouver, but British Columbia can do it.
